description:
Start with a real project

Match the exact item, pack size and variation to the Amazon listing. Record the supplier price and whether the listing has restrictions.

Review the first version

Check fees, shipping, prep and a lower selling-price scenario. Review historical signals alongside your own budget and expected sell-through.

Check the final result

Confirm restrictions and supplier terms before buying. Keep a short note explaining why you accepted or rejected each lead.

Frequently asked questions

Is an estimated profit enough to buy inventory?

Check the item match, actual costs, restrictions and what happens if the selling price falls.

Browse related tools on [SEOGBTools](https://seogbtools.com/).

Check the exact Amazon listing before running the numbers

Compare the supplier item with the listing photo, model, quantity, and package size. A single bottle and a two-pack can look similar at first glance. Record the listing ID and the reason you believe it matches. If the match is uncertain, leave the lead open until you can confirm it.

Estimate costs using the amount you actually pay for the item and any shipping or prep expenses you expect. Run a second estimate at a lower sale price. Ask whether the result still makes sense for your buying budget. Record the date and assumptions, and confirm selling eligibility in your own seller account before making a purchase.

Can I buy based on the first estimated margin?

Use the estimate to decide whether a lead deserves further review. Confirm the listing match, costs, selling restrictions, and what happens if the price falls.

Build a shortlist for Amazon product sourcing

Start with a marketplace and a category you already understand. Record each lead with the supplier, the exact item, the Amazon listing identifier, the date checked, and the available quantity. Keep the source URL or a supplier quote so you can retrace the figures when a price changes. Add a status such as “confirm pack size” or “verify eligibility” so someone reviewing the list can see the next action.

Separate the product match from the financial estimate. A low supplier price can look attractive even when the item differs from the listing. Compare the brand, model, variation, size, and number of units in the package. Read the listing title and the supplier description, then use packaging photos or product identifiers to check any unclear details. A retailer might sell a single item while the Amazon listing is for a set of two. In that case, even the right brand and color leave an important difference unresolved.

Verify selling eligibility in the correct marketplace

Select the same marketplace in SellerAmp SAS and your Amazon Seller Central account when reviewing eligibility. Then check the exact product in Seller Central before you commit inventory. A check for one account or marketplace cannot settle what a different account can sell. Record the marketplace and the date beside the result so you know which check you relied on.

If Amazon asks for approval, read the requirements that apply to the product and your account. Keep the lead pending until you understand what is needed and can confirm your status. A supplier's ability to ship the item and your ability to list it are separate checks.

Use the profit calculator to compare scenarios

Write down the expected selling price and the cost to put one sellable unit into inventory. Include the supplier price, shipping to you or your prep provider, and any packing or labeling cost you expect. Check the applicable Amazon fees for the intended fulfillment method. If the listing is a multipack, calculate your cost for the full pack. Use a consistent currency and record the date the figures were collected.

Run the same calculation at a second selling price that reflects a realistic downside. If a lead looks attractive at $24 but leaves almost no room at $21, write down the price at which the margin stops meeting your target. Those prices are examples. Use current listing and cost data for your own review. The point of the second estimate is to show which assumptions matter before you commit funds.

Review the decision before placing an order

Look at recent price and seller activity in context. A brief price increase may have little value if offers normally sell at a lower level. Review what you can verify about demand, how much stock you can afford to hold, and whether you can reorder later. Avoid using a single historical signal as a forecast of your own sales.

Write a short decision note for each lead. Include the listing match, confirmed eligibility, cost assumptions, and what would change the decision. If you reject a lead because the supplier item is a different pack, record that reason so the next reviewer can avoid repeating the same check.

**Public keyword candidates** SellerAmp group buy, Amazon product sourcing, Amazon profit calculator, product eligibility check.

Check the Amazon listing before checking profit

Search for the exact item by barcode or ASIN. Compare the pack size, model number, color, and condition against the supplier's page. A low price for one bottle means little if the Amazon listing is for a pack of two. Check the photos and the listing text together. If they disagree, find a listing you can match with confidence before you buy stock.

Check whether you can sell the product in your marketplace. Use your own Seller Central account to confirm any brand, category, or condition restrictions. A sourcing tool may help you notice a potential issue, but your ability to list the item depends on your account. Keep the supplier invoice and product identifiers with your sourcing notes.

Use the SellerAmp SAS profit calculator with your own costs

Enter what you actually expect to pay per sellable unit. Include supplier shipping, prep materials, and the cost to send stock to Amazon where they apply. A six-unit case that costs $48 plus $12 in shipping starts at $10 per unit before any other expense. If the listing is for a two-pack, your product cost starts at $20 per sellable pack.

Run the numbers at two sale prices. In an example with a $14 landed cost and $8 in estimated selling fees, a $30 sale leaves $8 before overhead and any additional costs. At $25, the same model leaves $3. That simple check shows how quickly a lead can become marginal. Use the current fee estimate for the actual listing and fulfillment method before placing an order.

Read the price history before choosing a quantity

Compare today's offer with what the listing has shown over time. A sudden price jump can reflect a short supply gap. If the price used to be lower when more sellers had stock, run your calculation at that lower price too. Check whether the chart covers the same variation and marketplace you plan to sell in. Save the date of your check so you know when to refresh it.

A small order can help you learn how quickly your offer sells and whether the prep takes longer than you expected. Set a maximum order size based on the cash you can tie up and the time you can afford to hold the stock. Keep the product on a watch list if the lead depends on a discount or an unusually high selling price.

Compare Amazon sourcing tools on the same product

Use one ASIN to compare SellerAmp SAS, a price-history tool, and Amazon's own fee calculator. Write down which screen answers each question. You might use SellerAmp to screen several leads, a historical chart to understand price changes, and Seller Central to confirm eligibility. Test a listing with a clear match first, then try a variation or multipack to see how easily you can spot errors.

Before choosing SellerAmp group buy access, check which marketplace and features are available, how usage is measured, and whether you can save your research privately. If you need browser tools or exports, confirm those details before ordering. Keep private account information and customer data in the systems your business controls.

Work through a sourcing decision from start to finish

Suppose you find a boxed kitchen scale at a supplier you already use. The supplier has eight units at a discount. The Amazon search results show a black scale, a silver scale, and a bundle that includes batteries. Before entering any costs, write down the manufacturer model number and verify that the Amazon detail page names that exact model. Check whether the battery pack is part of the item or a separate bundle. A match based on a picture alone can leave you with stock that belongs on another listing.

Next, open the offer list. Record the current selling price, the fulfillment method of the comparable offers, and the delivery dates a customer sees. If the lowest offer has a longer delivery time, it may be a poor reference for your planned offer. Use a conservative price that you would be comfortable accepting after other sellers adjust theirs. Enter the unit cost and fees for that price in your worksheet. Record the market and date so you can reproduce the calculation later.

Then ask how much work the order creates. Each scale might need a protective bag or a label. You may also need to inspect the battery compartment and confirm whether the supplier ships the units in retail packaging. Estimate the time to receive, check, label, and ship eight units. A lead with a small profit per unit may make sense if prep is quick and predictable. The same profit can be unattractive when each unit needs a separate inspection and the supplier takes two weeks to ship.

Finish by giving the lead one clear status. Buy a small test quantity if the listing match, eligibility, and numbers are sound. Put it on hold if a supplier detail remains unclear. Reject it if the math only works at an unusually high price. Write the reason in a sentence. When the same lead appears next month, you can update the details that changed and avoid repeating the entire search.

Decide which costs belong in the calculation

Separate costs you pay to get stock ready from costs you pay after a sale. Purchase price, supplier delivery, and prep are costs you usually know before you buy. Selling fees and fulfillment charges depend on the item, marketplace, and fulfillment method. A tool can help organize those inputs. The final estimate is only as good as the numbers you enter.

For online arbitrage, include the supplier's shipping threshold. A discount that assumes a larger basket may be unavailable on a one-unit test. For retail arbitrage, record the real checkout price and keep the receipt. For wholesale, check the minimum order quantity and whether shipping is included in the quote. If a supplier changes pack sizes or pricing tiers, recalculate using the units you can actually sell.

Set aside a place in your worksheet for costs that are uncertain. For example, storage costs can depend on how long the item stays in inventory. Returns can affect an item differently depending on whether it comes back in sellable condition. Use a reasonable allowance based on your own business experience, and keep that allowance visible. It is easier to improve a model when you know which numbers were estimates.

Compare return on investment with cash earned per sale

Return on investment helps you compare offers with different purchase costs. Profit per unit shows how much cash each completed sale could add after the costs in your model. Both numbers can be useful. A small item with a high percentage return can still earn very little per sale. A larger item with a lower percentage return can tie up cash longer and cost more to handle.

Consider two example leads. One requires $5 in inventory cost and might leave $2 after modeled costs. The other requires $20 and might leave $5. The first has the higher modeled return on inventory cost, while the second leaves more dollars per sale. If the first item needs extra prep or sells slowly, the higher percentage may matter less than it first appears. If the second item takes most of your budget, a bad price change could make it hard to fund other stock.

Use the same cost definitions when you compare leads. A return figure that includes supplier shipping should not be compared directly with one calculated from the shelf price alone. Check the numbers again after your first sales. Save the amount Amazon paid out and compare it with the earlier estimate. If there is a gap, trace it to a fee, cost, refund, or price change you can account for in the next sourcing round.

Build a repeatable check for offer and demand changes

Choose a few points in the price history and write down what you see at each one. Compare the normal price range with the price today. Look for times when more sellers appeared and the selling price fell. If you are looking at seasonal inventory, compare similar parts of the year where enough data exists. A short chart can be hard to interpret if it includes only a promotion or an out-of-stock period.

Use demand and rank signals to decide what to investigate. A rank estimate does not show how many units your specific offer will sell. Your price, stock, fulfillment, and competition can change the result. Look for a history that supports the size of your first order, then let your own sales and stock levels guide the reorder. If you have no reliable history for a listing, treat that as a reason to buy fewer units or wait for more evidence.

Keep a weekly note for active stock. Record units available, units sold, the current price, and the price you used when sourcing. If the available offers change sharply, look again before sending more inventory. Decide what you would do if the price reaches your break-even point. The best time to decide whether to hold or exit a lead is before you buy more of it.

Use a sourcing sheet that keeps evidence close to the decision

Create one row per product and link it to your supplier record. Add fields for ASIN, supplier model number, pack size, marketplace, landed cost, estimated fees, selling price, and the reason you chose that price. A second field for the date of the eligibility check helps when the same lead comes back. Store supplier documents where your team can retrieve them when needed.

Use short notes that another person can understand. “Price too low” tells them very little. “Pass below $24 because prep and inbound shipping reduce modeled profit to less than $2” gives a specific reason to recheck the product. If a teammate finds a cheaper supplier, they can rerun the calculation with that cost. If the seller count changes, they can check whether the price assumption still makes sense.

Keep personal login details and customer information out of shared notes. An ASIN, a public listing, and a dated cost estimate are usually enough for a teammate to review a lead. Keep invoices and sensitive business records in the accounts your team manages. Before using third-party access, check what data is visible, what can be exported, and what happens to saved research when access ends.

Common questions about Amazon product analysis

Can I use SellerAmp for a product I already sell?

Yes, a sourcing review can be useful before a reorder. Start with your own sales history and fees for that item. Then compare the current offers and supplier costs with the last time you purchased. If you have been selling at a different price from the one you originally modeled, use the price customers actually paid as part of the new decision.

Should I buy more when the current price is high?

Check how long the price has stayed high and what happened the last time additional sellers entered the listing. Make the estimate work at a price supported by the history. If the deal is only profitable at today's price, record the minimum sale price you need and decide whether the first order still fits your budget.

What if a supplier product has no exact listing match?

Confirm the brand, identifier, variation, and packaging. Do not rely on a similar photo or title. A different size or pack count can change both fees and what a customer expects. If the item would need a new listing, evaluate that as a separate project with its own demand assumptions and listing requirements.

How should I compare SellerAmp access options?

Make a short list of the tasks you need each week. It might include checking a barcode, reviewing price history, calculating fees for two markets, and exporting a lead. Check which of those tasks are available through the specific option you are considering, along with usage limits and support. If your work depends on private saved records or direct account controls, compare that requirement with the vendor's own subscription.
